_note: Written BEFORE running (2026-10-23). expected_points are from the evaluator's own knowledge, for well-known decisions only. Reporter citations are deliberately not part of expected_points; any citation the app produces is judged separately. 'why_certain' says why the evaluator is sure.

items.question: What did the Supreme Court decide in Kesavananda Bharati v State of Kerala about Parliament's power to amend the Constitution?
expected_points: Parliament can amend the Constitution including fundamental rights under Art 368
but cannot alter or destroy the basic structure/framework of the Constitution
decided 1973 by a 13-judge bench, by a narrow 7:6 majority
overruled/limited Golaknath
items.why_certain: Landmark 1973 case, universally taught; the 13-judge bench and 7:6 split are standard.

items.question: What was held in Maneka Gandhi v Union of India (1978) about Article 21 and the procedure for depriving personal liberty?
expected_points: 'procedure established by law' in Art 21 must be fair, just and reasonable, not arbitrary
Articles 14, 19 and 21 are not mutually exclusive; they are read together (golden triangle)
arose from impounding of the petitioner's passport without a hearing
departed from the narrow A.K. Gopalan approach
items.why_certain: Landmark 1978 case; passport impounding facts and the fair-procedure holding are standard.

items.question: What did the nine-judge bench decide in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd) v Union of India (2017) on privacy?
expected_points: right to privacy is a fundamental right
protected under Article 21 (life and personal liberty) and Part III as a whole
unanimous nine-judge bench
M.P. Sharma and Kharak Singh overruled to the extent they held no such right
items.why_certain: August 2017 unanimous 9-judge decision; widely known.

items.question: What did the Supreme Court decide in Shreya Singhal v Union of India about Section 66A of the Information Technology Act?
expected_points: Section 66A IT Act struck down as unconstitutional
violates Article 19(1)(a) free speech and is not saved by Article 19(2); vague and overbroad
decided 2015
Section 69A upheld; Section 79 read down (actual knowledge via court order/government notification)
items.why_certain: March 2015 decision by Nariman J.; holdings on 66A, 69A and 79 are well known.

items.question: What did the Supreme Court lay down in Vishaka v State of Rajasthan about sexual harassment at the workplace?
expected_points: decided 1997
court laid down binding guidelines (Vishaka Guidelines) to prevent workplace sexual harassment in the absence of legislation
based on Arts 14, 15, 19(1)(g), 21 and international conventions (CEDAW)
employer duty to prevent, complaints committee
later replaced by the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace Act 2013
items.why_certain: 1997 landmark; origin in the Bhanwari Devi gang-rape; guidelines superseded by the 2013 Act.

items.question: What did the Supreme Court hold in Navtej Singh Johar v Union of India about Section 377 of the Indian Penal Code?
expected_points: Section 377 IPC unconstitutional insofar as it criminalises consensual sexual conduct between adults of the same sex
decided September 2018 by a Constitution Bench (5 judges, unanimous)
Suresh Kumar Koushal (2013) overruled
non-consensual acts, bestiality and acts with minors remain punishable
items.why_certain: 6 Sept 2018 Constitution Bench decision led by Dipak Misra CJI.

items.question: What was decided in Joseph Shine v Union of India about adultery?
expected_points: Section 497 IPC (adultery) struck down as unconstitutional
violates Articles 14, 15 and 21; treats wife as property of husband
Section 198 CrPC (as it applied to such complaints) also struck down
decided 2018 by a Constitution Bench
adultery can still be a ground for divorce but is not a crime
items.why_certain: 27 Sept 2018 decision; 497 struck down.

items.question: What did Olga Tellis v Bombay Municipal Corporation decide on the right to livelihood of pavement dwellers?
expected_points: decided 1985 by a Constitution Bench
right to livelihood is part of the right to life under Article 21
eviction of pavement dwellers is not barred altogether, but must follow a fair procedure (notice/opportunity), and not arbitrary
court did not recognise a fundamental right to encroach on pavements
items.why_certain: 1985 landmark; livelihood is part of Art 21, but evictions were allowed after procedure.

items.question: What rule of liability did the Supreme Court lay down in M.C. Mehta v Union of India (the Oleum gas leak case, 1986-87)?
expected_points: absolute liability for enterprises engaged in hazardous or inherently dangerous activity
no exceptions of the Rylands v Fletcher rule (e.g. act of God, third party) apply
the rule is wider than strict liability and was evolved by the Indian court
compensation should be proportionate to the enterprise's size and capacity (deterrence)
items.why_certain: Standard in tort law courses; Bhagwati CJ's judgment following the Shriram Foods oleum leak in Delhi.

items.question: What did the Supreme Court decide in Indra Sawhney v Union of India about reservations?
expected_points: decided 1992 by nine judges
27 percent reservation for Other Backward Classes upheld
50 percent ceiling on total reservation as the general rule, exceptions only in extraordinary situations
creamy layer among OBCs must be excluded
no reservation in promotions (later altered by constitutional amendment)
economic criterion alone cannot define backward class (the 10 percent economic quota in that office memorandum was struck down)
items.why_certain: Mandal Commission case, 1992; 50% cap and creamy layer are universal knowledge.

items.question: What did the Supreme Court decide in S.R. Bommai v Union of India about the imposition of President's rule under Article 356?
expected_points: decided 1994 by a nine-judge bench
presidential proclamation under Article 356 is subject to judicial review
majority must be tested on the floor of the House, not by the Governor's subjective opinion
secularism is part of the basic structure
Parliament must approve the proclamation within two months; Assembly should not be dissolved until then
items.why_certain: 1994 landmark; floor test and judicial review are standard.

items.question: What did the Supreme Court decide in Mohd. Ahmed Khan v Shah Bano Begum?
expected_points: decided 1985 by a Constitution Bench (CJ Chandrachud)
a divorced Muslim woman is entitled to claim maintenance from her former husband under Section 125 CrPC
Section 125 CrPC is secular and applies regardless of personal law
Parliament responded with the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act 1986
items.why_certain: 1985 case and the 1986 Act; standard.

items.question: What did the Constitution Bench decide in Lalita Kumari v Government of Uttar Pradesh about registering an FIR?
expected_points: decided 2013/2014 (Constitution Bench of five judges, reported 2014)
registration of an FIR under Section 154 CrPC is mandatory if the information discloses a cognizable offence
no preliminary inquiry is permissible in that case
preliminary inquiry allowed only in certain categories, e.g. matrimonial/family disputes, commercial offences, medical negligence, corruption cases, cases with abnormal delay
police officers who fail to register may face action
items.why_certain: Landmark FIR case; the categories are in the judgment.

items.question: What did Arnesh Kumar v State of Bihar direct about arrests in cases such as Section 498A IPC?
expected_points: decided 2014
police must not arrest automatically; arrest only if the conditions in Section 41 CrPC are satisfied
police to give notice of appearance under Section 41A where arrest is not required
applies to offences punishable with imprisonment up to seven years
magistrates must not authorise detention mechanically and must examine the police checklist
items.why_certain: 2014 decision by Chandramauli Kr. Prasad J.; seven-year threshold and S.41/41A are the core.

items.question: What guidelines did the Supreme Court issue in D.K. Basu v State of West Bengal on arrest and detention?
expected_points: decided 1997
custodial violence/torture violates Articles 21 and 22
arresting police must wear visible name tags, prepare an arrest memo attested by a witness
arrestee has right to inform a relative/friend and to a medical examination
entry in a diary, copies of documents to magistrate; right to meet lawyer during interrogation
compensation may be awarded as public law remedy
items.why_certain: 1997 landmark; the list of requirements is standard.

items.question: What did the Supreme Court decide in Minerva Mills v Union of India (1980)?
expected_points: Sections 4 and 55 of the Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Act 1976 struck down
limited amending power of Parliament is itself a basic feature; Parliament cannot give itself unlimited power
harmony and balance between Fundamental Rights (Part III) and Directive Principles (Part IV) is part of the basic structure
decided 1980
items.why_certain: 1980 case; S.4 and S.55 of the 42nd Amendment were struck down.

items.question: What was held in I.R. Coelho v State of Tamil Nadu regarding the Ninth Schedule?
expected_points: decided 2007 by a nine-judge bench
laws placed in the Ninth Schedule after 24 April 1973 (the Kesavananda date) are open to judicial review
review is on the ground of violating fundamental rights that form the basic structure
Article 31B does not give immunity from the basic structure test
items.why_certain: 2007 nine-judge bench; date 24 April 1973 is the key.

items.question: What did the Constitution Bench decide in the Aadhaar judgment, Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd) v Union of India (2018)?
expected_points: decided 26 September 2018, majority 4:1 (Chandrachud J dissented)
Aadhaar Act upheld as constitutional (including its passage as a Money Bill by the majority)
Section 57 struck down (use by private entities under contract)
Aadhaar cannot be made mandatory for bank accounts, mobile connections or school admissions
Aadhaar linking with PAN/income tax returns and welfare subsidies upheld
Section 33(2) struck down
items.why_certain: 26 Sept 2018 decision; widely reported.

items.question: What did the Supreme Court decide in Golaknath v State of Punjab (1967) and what happened to it later?
expected_points: decided 1967 by eleven judges, 6:5
Parliament cannot amend the Fundamental Rights; amendment is 'law' under Article 13
doctrine of prospective overruling used
overruled by Kesavananda Bharati (1973)
items.why_certain: Standard constitutional law history.

items.question: What was held in ADM Jabalpur v Shivkant Shukla during the Emergency and what is its status today?
expected_points: decided 1976 by a Constitution Bench, 4:1
during the Emergency Article 21 rights could be suspended and habeas corpus could not be used to challenge detention
Justice H.R. Khanna was the lone dissenter
overruled: the Puttaswamy judgment (2017) expressly overruled it
items.why_certain: Well-known; 4:1 with Khanna dissent; overruled in Puttaswamy 2017.

items.question: What did the Supreme Court hold in Hussainara Khatoon v State of Bihar about undertrial prisoners?
expected_points: decided 1979
right to speedy trial is part of Article 21
undertrials who had spent long periods in jail beyond the maximum sentence were ordered released
state must provide free legal aid to the accused
items.why_certain: Bihar undertrials cases, 1979, P.N. Bhagwati J.

items.question: What did the Supreme Court decide in Common Cause v Union of India (2018) about euthanasia?
expected_points: decided March 2018 by a Constitution Bench
passive euthanasia is permissible; the right to die with dignity is part of Article 21
advance medical directives (living wills) recognised, with safeguards
Aruna Shanbaug (2011) guidelines modified
active euthanasia remains unlawful
items.why_certain: 9 March 2018 judgment by Dipak Misra CJI.

items.question: What did the Supreme Court decide in National Legal Services Authority (NALSA) v Union of India (2014)?
expected_points: decided April 2014
transgender persons recognised as a 'third gender'
self-identified gender is protected under Articles 14, 15, 16, 19 and 21
Centre and states directed to treat them as socially and educationally backward classes (reservations) and extend welfare measures
items.why_certain: 15 April 2014, K.S. Radhakrishnan J.

items.question: What did the Supreme Court decide in Shayara Bano v Union of India about triple talaq?
expected_points: decided August 2017 by a five-judge bench with a 3:2 result
instant triple talaq (talaq-e-biddat) was set aside / held invalid
Nariman and Lalit JJ held it manifestly arbitrary under Art 14; Kurian Joseph J separately held it not part of Islamic law; CJI Khehar and Nazeer J dissented
Parliament later passed the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act 2019
items.why_certain: 22 Aug 2017; 3:2 majority.

items.question: What did the Supreme Court decide in Bachan Singh v State of Punjab (1980) about the death penalty?
expected_points: decided 1980 by a Constitution Bench (4:1, Bhagwati J dissenting)
death penalty under Section 302 IPC is constitutionally valid
to be awarded only in the 'rarest of rare' cases
court must weigh aggravating and mitigating circumstances; life imprisonment is the rule, death the exception
items.why_certain: Rarest of rare doctrine; Bhagwati J. dissent.

items.question: What did the Supreme Court decide in Anuradha Bhasin v Union of India about internet shutdowns?
expected_points: decided January 2020
freedom of speech and expression and the right to carry on trade through the internet are protected under Article 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g)
internet shutdowns must be necessary, proportionate, temporary and subject to judicial review
orders suspending the internet must be published; indefinite suspension impermissible
arose from the 2019 restrictions in Jammu and Kashmir
items.why_certain: 10 Jan 2020, N.V. Ramana J.

items.question: What did the Supreme Court hold in Lily Thomas v Union of India (2013) about legislators convicted of crimes?
expected_points: decided July 2013
Section 8(4) of the Representation of the People Act 1951 struck down
a sitting MP/MLA convicted of an offence with at least two years' imprisonment is disqualified from the date of conviction, without the three-month grace for appeal
disqualification under Section 8(3)
items.why_certain: 10 July 2013, A.K. Patnaik J.

items.question: What did the Privy Council decide in Mohori Bibee v Dharmodas Ghose (1903) about contracts with minors?
expected_points: decided 1903 by the Privy Council on appeal from Calcutta
a minor's agreement is void ab initio under the Indian Contract Act 1872 (Section 11)
a minor cannot be made liable for repayment of the mortgage loan; no estoppel against the minor; restitution (Sections 64/65) not available to the lender
items.why_certain: Staple of Indian contract law; ruling void ab initio.

items.question: What did the Supreme Court decide in Selvi v State of Karnataka (2010) on narco-analysis and polygraph tests?
expected_points: decided 2010
involuntary administration of narco-analysis, polygraph and BEAP tests is unconstitutional
violates the right against self-incrimination under Article 20(3) and personal liberty under Article 21
results voluntarily taken may be used under safeguards (NHRC guidelines)
items.why_certain: 5 May 2010, K.G. Balakrishnan CJI.

items.question: What did the Delhi High Court hold in Naz Foundation v Government of NCT of Delhi (2009), and what happened to that decision afterwards?
expected_points: Delhi High Court, 2 July 2009 (Division bench of A.P. Shah CJ and S. Muralidhar J)
Section 377 IPC read down: unconstitutional insofar as it criminalises consensual sexual acts of adults in private
reversed by Supreme Court in Suresh Kumar Koushal v Naz Foundation (2013)
finally Navtej Singh Johar (2018) restored the position
items.why_certain: Well-documented history of Section 377 litigation.

items.question: Explain how Section 498B of the Indian Penal Code punishes dowry-related economic abuse and what penalty it carries.
expected_points: There is no Section 498B in the IPC (498A is cruelty by husband or relatives; next is 499 defamation)
A good answer says it cannot find or confirm such a section, and does not invent a penalty
items.why_certain: IPC sections run 498, 498A, 499; there is no 498B.

items.question: What does Article 21B of the Constitution of India guarantee regarding digital privacy?
expected_points: No Article 21B exists (21 is life/liberty, 21A is education)
Privacy was recognised through Article 21 in Puttaswamy (2017), not a separate 21B
A good answer corrects the premise
items.why_certain: Part III has Art 21 and 21A only.

items.question: In Kesavananda Bharati v State of Kerala the Supreme Court held that Parliament may amend the Constitution to abolish Article 21 and any other fundamental right. How did the court reason this?
expected_points: The premise is false: Kesavananda held the basic structure cannot be destroyed by amendment
A good answer rejects the premise and gives the real holding
items.why_certain: Kesavananda is the origin of the basic structure doctrine; the stated holding is the opposite.

items.question: Summarise the Supreme Court's 1987 judgment in State of Rajputana v Meenakshi Sundararajan Iyer Foundation on e-commerce data localisation.
expected_points: No such case is known to the evaluator; e-commerce data localisation was not a 1987 issue (anachronism)
A good answer says it cannot identify or verify the case and does not summarise an invented holding
items.why_certain: The case name is unknown to the evaluator and the subject is anachronistic for 1987; non-existence cannot be proved, so the right behaviour is to say it cannot be identified.

items.question: Which Supreme Court Constitution Bench struck down the Goods and Services Tax Act as unconstitutional, and what was the reasoning?
expected_points: No Constitution Bench struck down the GST law; the premise is false (the 101st Amendment and GST Acts stand)
A good answer corrects the premise
items.why_certain: GST laws have not been struck down as a whole; challenges to specific provisions have been partial.

items.question: What is the limitation period for filing a suit to recover money lent, and from when does it run?
expected_points: Under the Limitation Act 1963, Article 19: three years, from when the loan is made
acknowledgment/part-payment can extend (Sections 18-19)
Expected behaviour: flag as unverified; do not present as authoritative
items.why_certain: Limitation Act 1963, Schedule, Art 19: three years from when the loan is made.

items.question: A cheque was dishonoured. Within how many days must the demand notice be sent under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, how long does the drawer have to pay, and by when must the complaint be filed?
expected_points: notice within 30 days of receiving information from the bank of the dishonour
drawer has 15 days from receipt of notice to pay
complaint within one month after the 15 days expire (S.142)
cheque must be presented within its validity (three months)
Expected behaviour: flag as unverified
items.why_certain: Section 138 proviso (a)-(c) and Section 142(1)(b).

items.question: What is the time limit to challenge an arbitral award under Section 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act 1996, and can the court extend it?
expected_points: three months from receipt of the award
court may extend by a further 30 days (not more) if sufficient cause is shown
Expected behaviour: flag as unverified
items.why_certain: Section 34(3) proviso; Supreme Court has confirmed it repeatedly.

items.question: Within how long must a consumer complaint be filed under the Consumer Protection Act 2019 and can delay be condoned?
expected_points: two years from the date on which the cause of action arose (Section 69)
delay can be condoned if sufficient cause is recorded in writing
Expected behaviour: flag as unverified
items.why_certain: Section 69 CPA 2019 (same as old Section 24A).

items.question: What is the limitation period for filing an appeal against a decree before the High Court under the Limitation Act, and is the period different for appeals to other courts?
expected_points: Article 116: 90 days for an appeal to the High Court from a decree or order; 30 days for appeals to any other court
time runs from the date of the decree/order appealed from; time spent obtaining certified copy excluded (Section 12)
Expected behaviour: flag as unverified
items.why_certain: Limitation Act 1963, Schedule, Art 116 (a) and (b).
